curation.why: lexical_declaration is a `const`/`let` statement, and at 7 occurrences it was the most frequent proposal. It looked like a container because `const apply = (amount) => {...}` genuinely nests an arrow function below it, but it names nothing itself — the variable_declarator holds the name one level down, and the arrow_function is the real body. Anchoring on it would add a level to every trail that passes through a const binding. Dropped as a landmark but kept as a `variable` label so a query summary still names it. function_expression is added as a landmark: it is the `function () {}` form used as a value (a callback, an IIFE, an event handler), and the sample does not happen to contain one because modern JavaScript prefers arrow functions — adding one purely to satisfy the generator would be sample padding. It is a real function body worth bookmarking inside, and it is labelled `function` so it resolves as a container like the other function forms. Note the contrast with Python's lambda and Rust's closure_expression, which can *never* be proposed: an arrow_function has a body, so the generator does propose it from the samples, and only function_expression needs declaring here. `function` is added as a container even though the generator already proposed it — it is kept explicit because arrow_function carries that label and has no name field, so like a Zig struct_declaration it anchors a query and sticks while scrolling while the breadcrumb renderer skips it. field_definition is labelled `variable` so a class field reads the same as a top-level binding; it is deliberately not a landmark, since a field is reached through the class that declares it. The remaining add_labels carry no landmark or container weight and exist purely so a query summary reads in JavaScript's own vocabulary: while_statement and do_statement (the generator observed only for_statement and for_in_statement). There is deliberately no `for_of_statement` entry: this grammar parses `for (const x of xs)` as a for_in_statement, which the generator already labelled `for loop`, and naming the kind that reads naturally is a lint error (`node kind 'for_of_statement' is not defined by this grammar, did you mean 'for_in_statement'?`) rather than a silent no-op, switch_case alongside the switch_statement and switch_default it already labelled, try_statement/catch_clause/ternary_expression as `if statement` since the label set has no dedicated exception or ternary concept and these are the closest sanctioned fit, and new_expression as `call` because `new Invoice(...)` is a use site rather than a declaration. Unlike Java, this grammar does have a real `switch_statement` kind, so no workaround is needed there.
